title: Sequential decisions and dynamic programming
summary: States, actions, policies and long-term objectives. Solve a small route-planning problem by backward induction.
objectives: Model a sequential decision problem using states, actions, transitions and costs.
Distinguish a policy from a fixed action sequence.
Explain backward induction and the connection between DP and RL.
reading: Bertsekas, Dynamic Programming and Optimal Control, Volume I, Chapter 1; Sutton and Barto, Chapter 1.

title: Finite-horizon DP and shortest paths
summary: The principle of optimality, deterministic finite-state models, and backward computation on a layered graph.
objectives: Write a finite-horizon Bellman recursion with a terminal condition.
Recover an optimal policy from a value table.
Compare enumeration with dynamic programming.

title: Stochastic dynamic programming
summary: Random transitions, feedback policies, and expected total cost in inventory and stopping problems.
objectives: Explain why feedback matters under uncertainty.
Calculate an expected cost-to-go.
Build and solve a small stochastic DP model.

title: Infinite-horizon problems
summary: Discounting, stationary policies, Bellman equations, and the intuition behind contraction.
objectives: Explain the role of a discount factor.
Formulate an infinite-horizon discounted MDP.
Connect finite-horizon recursions to a fixed-point equation.
reading: Sutton and Barto, Chapter 3; MIT 6.231 infinite-horizon lectures.

title: Value iteration and policy iteration
summary: Policy evaluation, policy improvement, and algorithms for solving a known finite MDP.
objectives: Implement value iteration and policy iteration.
Distinguish evaluation from control.
Interpret stopping criteria and approximation error.

title: Approximate DP and online planning
summary: Approximate value functions, online search and rollout for problems where exact DP is too costly, followed by a brief introduction to partial observations.
objectives: Explain how approximate values reduce the cost of planning.
Work through a short lookahead search and a rollout using a base policy.
Recognize when an augmented or belief state is needed under partial observations.
reading: Selected MIT 6.231 lectures on imperfect information and approximate DP.

title: Lab 1: resource-constrained path planning
summary: Use an expanded state to plan a route under a resource budget and examine computational tradeoffs.
objectives: Design a state representation that includes a resource budget.
Implement and check a DP solution on a small instance.
Explain feasibility, optimality and computational cost.
reading: Review Lectures 2, 3 and 6. Any confirmed lab instructions will appear on the Assignments page.

title: Bandits, exploration and regret
summary: Learning from sampled experience, exploration versus exploitation, and regret in multi-armed bandits. Compare epsilon-greedy exploration, optimism and Thompson sampling.
objectives: Distinguish planning with a model from learning through interaction.
Estimate action values and calculate cumulative regret in a small bandit example.
Explain the intuition behind upper confidence bounds and Thompson sampling.
reading: Sutton and Barto, Chapters 1-2; Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Algorithms, selected material on bandits and exploration.

title: Monte Carlo methods
summary: Learning values from complete episodes, Monte Carlo control, and on-policy versus off-policy data.
objectives: Estimate a value from sampled returns.
Explain policy improvement using estimated action values.
Describe the difference between behavior and target policies.

title: Temporal-difference learning and control
summary: Bootstrapping, TD prediction, SARSA and Q-learning in a common tabular environment, with a short comparison of one-step, n-step and Monte Carlo targets.
objectives: Explain the TD error and bootstrapping.
Implement SARSA and Q-learning.
Compare on-policy and off-policy control.
Relate n-step returns to the one-step TD and Monte Carlo targets.
reading: Sutton and Barto, Chapter 6; Chapter 7 for the optional n-step extension.

title: Multi-agent reinforcement learning
summary: Cooperation and competition in games, equilibrium concepts, and a first look at learning in Markov games. Introduce centralized training with decentralized execution at a conceptual level.
objectives: Distinguish cooperative, competitive and mixed-motive interactions.
Find best responses and an equilibrium in a small matrix game.
Explain why other learning agents make the environment nonstationary.
Distinguish centralized training from decentralized execution.
reading: Selected lecture notes on matrix games, Markov games and introductory multi-agent reinforcement learning; specific readings will be announced.

title: Function approximation and deep Q-learning
summary: Generalization beyond value tables, linear approximation, and key design choices in deep Q-learning.
objectives: Represent a value function with features or a neural network.
Explain replay and target networks.
Recognize instability risks when approximation and bootstrapping interact.
reading: Sutton and Barto, Chapters 9-11; selected Stanford CS234 materials.

title: Policy gradients and actor-critic methods
summary: Direct policy optimization, REINFORCE, variance reduction and actor-critic methods.
objectives: Explain how a stochastic policy can be optimized directly.
Interpret a policy-gradient estimate and the role of a baseline.
Distinguish the actor and critic in an actor-critic method.
reading: Sutton and Barto, Chapter 13; Stanford CS224R policy-gradient lectures.

title: Reinforcement learning for language models
summary: Text generation as a decision process, preference feedback, verifiable rewards, and an introduction to RLHF and reasoning.
objectives: Map language generation to states, actions, policies and rewards.
Distinguish preference-based feedback from verifiable outcome rewards.
Explain the role of reward models and regularization in post-training.
reading: Stanford CS224R 2026, Lectures 9-10; Berkeley CS285 2026, Lecture 14.

title: Lab 2: learning for sequential decisions
summary: Evaluate learned policies on a small dynamic decision problem; an LLM-related extension is an optional project direction.
objectives: Choose suitable baselines and evaluation metrics.
Report results across multiple runs.
Analyze the limitations of a learned policy.
reading: Review Lectures 8-14. Any confirmed lab instructions will appear on the Assignments page.

title: Synthesis and project discussion
summary: Connect modeling, planning, learning and approximation; discuss experiments and revisit the semester's core ideas. Optional outlook topics include risk-aware decisions, offline RL and continual learning, as time permits.
objectives: Select an appropriate method for a sequential decision problem.
Explain the assumptions and limitations of that method.
Connect dynamic programming to modern reinforcement learning.
reading: Review lecture notes and any completed practice exercises. Scheduling depends on the verified makeup arrangement.
